claims.claim: The user stated the scope, the desired behaviour, and the location
claims.evidence: Checked against the eval prompt. Scope: "Should be a small change." Behaviour: "prints what it would do instead of doing it." Location: "the sync command." All three quotes are accurate.

claims.claim: 'The eval framing also forbids clarifying questions'
claims.evidence: References harness instructions not present in the supplied artifacts, so unverifiable here. It is also a leak of eval-harness awareness into the routing rationale — the run is partly reasoning about being evaluated rather than about the task, though it immediately disclaims dependence on it ("but I would not have asked here regardless").

claims.claim: --dry-run strictly reduces the blast radius, so there is no new attack surface
claims.evidence: Sound as stated for the purpose it serves (declining security-and-hardening and /review). A dry-run path that diverges from the real path can mislead, but the run separately guards that: "Keep the read/compute path identical so the printed plan is truthful rather than a separate code path."

claims.claim: This is one edit in one or two files
claims.evidence: Asserted without having read any code — no repository was inspected in this run. The run itself hedges this later: it would escalate if "side effects [are] scattered across many call sites so the change is not in fact small." Reasonable prior, not a verified fact.

claims.claim: No code was written; the run stops at 'let me look at how the command is wired up first'
claims.evidence: response.md is 212 characters and contains no diff, file path, or edit. Consistent with a routing-only eval, but no expectation tests implementation quality.

suggestions.expectation: Says explicitly that the heavier chain is being skipped because the change is small
suggestions.reason: This run passes entirely on the strength of routing.md; its user-facing response.md (212 chars) never says the change is small or that process is being skipped. If the intent is that the *user* hears the rationale, the expectation should name response.md as the location — otherwise it grades an artifact the user never sees, and a run could pass while telling the user nothing.

suggestions.expectation: Routes to test-driven-development, or proceeds directly, rather than to a multi-skill chain
suggestions.reason: The disjunction is broad enough that a run invoking nothing at all and a run routing to TDD both pass. Since a baseline with no skill loaded satisfies it by default, it cannot discriminate skill-driven routing from the absence of routing.

suggestions.expectation: Names at most two skills in total
suggestions.reason: Read literally this expectation fails every strong answer — this run names 16 skills and commands, all to reject them, which is the behaviour the eval wants. It is only gradeable under the counting convention supplied in the grader prompt. Reword to 'commits to invoking at most two skills' so the criterion is self-contained.

No expectation covers the quality of the proposed change, and this run stops before reading any code. Its most valuable engineering observation — "Keep the read/compute path identical so the printed plan is truthful rather than a separate code path" — and its escalation condition are entirely uncaught by the rubric. An expectation on identifying that --dry-run must suppress every side effect and must not fork into a separate code path would be discriminating.

The run reasons about the eval harness itself ("The eval framing also forbids clarifying questions"). Harness awareness leaking into routing rationale is worth an explicit negative check, since it can substitute for genuine task judgment.

eval_feedback.overall: All four expectations pass. The rubric confirms ceremony was avoided but does not test whether the plan is any good, and expectations 2 and 3 are satisfied trivially by a baseline that simply invokes nothing — which is precisely what happened here.
